#1942. Mauricio Pochettino is adored by his players, big on culture and good vibes, not afraid to crack the whip and does not suffer fools - exactly what dysfunctional Man United are crying out for

By KIERAN GILL, MAIL SPORT REPORTER and MATT BARLOW, FOOTBALL WRITER and DANIEL MATTHEWS, US SENIOR SPORTS WRITER

Published: 17:59 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 18:01 EST, 10 November 2026

After one press conference during Mauricio Pochettino’s ill-fated spell at Chelsea, he hosted an Argentinian-style BBQ for approximately 130 people, including his players and their families, under a marquee set up in the first-team car park at their training ground.

Returning to the room and the assembled throng of journalists still working, Pochettino popped a large plate of sausages and steaks down on the desk. He insisted it did not constitute bribery for better coverage of him. Just thought we might like to join.

This was Pochettino personified. Big on togetherness. Insisted on creating a homely environment for everyone. Believed a harmonious culture at Cobham would help performances on the pitch. Even kept a big box of lemons in his office because he reckoned they harnessed ‘energia universal’. He emphasised the importance of a good mood.

Goodness knows that’s what Manchester United need right now. And if they do decide to dismiss Michael Carrick, the prospect of managing possibly the biggest club in world football would not faze Pochettino – now the bookies’ favourite to take over.

Indeed, the 54-year-old would relish the challenge.

A few days before USA’s World Cup victory against Bosnia and Herzegovina to reach the last 16 at this summer’s tournament, coach Pochettino invited a small group of journalists to interview him at the team hotel – the Ritz-Carlton in Laguna Niguel, overlooking the Pacific Ocean 50 miles south of Los Angeles.

Manchester United could do with a dose of Mauricio Pochettino - and he would relish the challenge

The United States manager - who would cost around £7.5million to release - has openly admitted he wants to lead them in the future

Towards the end of the interview the Manchester United job came up in conversation. Pochettino turned to his long-time assistant coach Jesus Perez and said: ‘One day, your dream comes true... you go to Manchester United!’.

The Argentine clarified somewhat by explaining that Perez, while living in London, would often visit Manchester on days off to visit the National Football Museum. Perez responded with a smile: ‘United should have got you’.

One thing about Pochettino that Manchester United players will soon figure out if he takes the reins at Old Trafford is that he is not afraid to crack the whip and does not suffer fools. At the World Cup, he appeared to criticise the intervention of FIFA - and President Trump – in suspending Folarin Balogun’s ban to make the striker available for a knockout clash with Belgium.

‘I feel disappointed with too many people. They put politics and manipulation, talk about ethics and integrity [first]. If we talk about the history of this game, I am disappointed in a personal way.’

With Pochettino, you’re either all in or you’re out. Look back to his time at Tottenham for evidence of that: the decision to exile stars such as Younes Kaboul, Etienne Capoue and Paulinho into a ‘bomb squad’ - and give chances to stars such as Harry Kane - was the start of his success there.

He’s a builder of teams, works with the tools he has and makes players better. Again, that sounds like the sort of thing United are crying out for.

Pochettino is big on culture – he adopted the mantra ‘culture eats strategy for breakfast’ after a meeting with the chairman of U.S. fast food chain Chick-fil-A – and worked hard to change the holiday camp feel at the USA team. Senior stars believed they did not need to put in the extra work to keep their places. The most notable example saw national team poster-boy Christian Pulisic, once of Chelsea, attempt to skip key games after a long season for AC Milan. Pochettino put a stop to that.

The Argentine does not suffer fools, is big on culture, and can deal with big club executives - his time at Tottenham taught us that

He can manage upwards, too. He handled chairman Daniel Levy well, and credited open dialogue as being key to the partnership with the chairman which yielded a runners-up finish in the Premier League and a run to the Champions League final.

‘I speak to him a lot, we talk a lot, we have very good communication,’ Pochettino said in 2018.

‘That means sometimes we agree and sometimes we don't agree. But after, when the decision is made, we are so strong in the delivery of it which shows it is best for the club’.

His cordial relationship with Levy meant Spurs were unconcerned when he met Sir Alex Ferguson in 2016 at Scott’s in Mayfair towards the end of Louis van Gaal’s troubled reign at Old Trafford.

There was nothing untoward in that - after the restaurant meeting Pochettino returned to Spurs training, and United appointed Jose Mourinho that summer.

But he was again touted as a contender when Mourinho was dismissed two years later.

Levy sacked him in 2019, but Pochettino has remained respectful and has since praised Levy’s impact.

On the field, his time at Spurs became famous for relentless intensity - a high energy approach with a high press. Think flying full-backs Danny Rose and Kyle Walker, and all-action midfielder Mousa Dembele. For another example of him getting the best from players look at Cole Palmer. The Englishman has never since replicated his numbers from 2023-24, Pochettino’s only season at Stamford Bridge.

The football, admittedly, was a little chaotic at Chelsea. It lacked control, and not even a mountain of meat could prevent him from being quizzed about his style of play in press conferences.

Chelsea’s fans never took to Pochettino. He was the face of Spurs, after all. Pochettino might be walking his dog – a Rhodesian Ridgeback called Sansa, named after the Game of Thrones character Sansa Stark – and the odd supporter would happily stop him to have a cosy chat. But he was always going to struggle to win over the supporters in their entirety.

He once said the first time he felt a connection with Chelsea’s supporters was in April 2024 after defeating Erik Ten Hag’s United 4-3, when Cole Palmer scored twice in the 10th and 11th minutes of stoppage time. That was 11 months after he joined.

He never quite won over the fanbase of Chelsea, where his football was chaotic and his high-intensity values led to accusations that he had worsened their injury crisis

One source at the time said Pochettino wanted ‘machines’ who had the physicality to play the high-energy philosophy he craved, and like at Spurs there was indeed a great deal of high-intensity running involved in training.

However, this talk of his sessions being fitness-focused led to accusations that his methods were contributing to their crippling injury list. Pochettino disputed that, telling us he did not come ‘from Mars’ and that he knew how to manage footballers better than those on social media. He was extremely defensive whenever asked if his training was primitive.

It would be fair to debate whether United have the players to play this way – and indeed how Pochettino himself would respond to the changing landscape of the Premier League.

Spurs boss Roberto de Zerbi noted recently that upon his return to the Premier League after two years away that almost all clubs now play a more physical game than when he was at Brighton. With more teams doing the same thing that once made a Pochettino side different, how would he adapt?

We are told leaving his job in charge of the USA is more contractually feasible now than it was before the 2026 World Cup when Spurs made checks last season. He has a buyout clause, apparently worth around £7million, though that does not include the compensation required to recruit Perez and Co.

Should United require any character references, they need only ask their own Luke Shaw. He wrote the epilogue of Guillem Balague’s book Brave New World: Inside Pochettino’s Spurs, having played under him at Southampton. Shaw admitted in those pages that he would love to work with his old coach again someday. Pochettino was there for him when Shaw broke his leg – still a man-manager even when they were no longer working together.

But United could also ask any number of Chelsea players who worked with Pochettino. They largely loved him. At the time of his dismissal in May 2024, one agent of a senior figure in the changing room told us that their client was ‘devastated’. Nicolas Jackson, formerly of Chelsea and now of Aston Villa, responded to Pochettino leaving by posting two face-palm emojis on Instagram.

Pochettino had his favourites. Conor Gallagher was one of them, and the Cobham graduate's contractual situation seemed to be a source of angst between the coach and Chelsea’s hierarchy.

Players tend to love Pochettino - Luke Shaw (right), one of Manchester United's veterans, had a strong relationship with him at Southampton

His power waned at Chelsea - the club hired a set-piece coach after he insisted he didn't want one, and he was gone before the specialist arrived

As noted, Pochettino was a builder hired to work with one of the Premier League’s youngest squads but did not get the time he wanted to mould Chelsea and never hid his desire for more power at Stamford Bridge. It is said they once had the chance to sign Ansu Fati from Barcelona on favourable financial terms, but did not go through with the transfer after the manager decided he was not for him.

We did get a glimpse of Pochettino’s waning power when Daily Mail Sport asked him once whether he would like a set-piece specialist adding to his staff. He dismissed the idea, suggesting he did not need one. Chelsea then lost the Carabao Cup final when Liverpool’s Virgil van Dijk headed in the winner in extra time from a corner, with Gary Neville coining the ‘blue billion-pound bottlejobs’ jibe.

A month later, Chelsea agreed a deal to hire Bernardo Cueva from Brentford to lead a new department dedicated to set-pieces. Pochettino responded by reminding us: ‘I am the head coach and I am going to decide if some people are going to be with me or not, or if I’m going to add more people or not to the touchline.’ He was gone before Cueva arrived in the summer.

An end-of-season review was held in May 2024, and Pochettino, along with Chelsea’s hierarchy, decided after a single season that it was not working. Not for him, and not for them.

Now those at the helm of United need to determine whether he is the man to bring the good vibes back, perhaps also with a little meat.

#1941. Scotland half-centurion issues Pocognoli warning and reveals why misfiring striker should keep starting berth

Sebastien Pocognoli will need time to fully implement his ideas in Scotland’s new look squad, but has been warned fans will want to see signs of progress in the upcoming Nations League games this week.

Pocognoli, 39, had a mixed start to his tenure as Scotland’s new head coach, losing to both Switzerland and Slovenia at Hampden Park, drawing away to Slovenia and winning just one of their opening Nations League games with a 2-0 away win against North Macedonia.

Handing international debuts to no less than five players in his maiden camp as Scotland head coach, the Belgian boss has shown no fear when it comes to introducing fresh faces to his pack. However, he came under scrutiny for his willingness to adopt a back three formation, with many pundits questioning whether the team has the personnel to adapt.

Curious to see what he has learned from last month’s games, 50-cap former Scotland international Alan Hutton thinks it will take time for the team to adapt to his methods, but would like to see improved performances against North Macedonia and Switzerland over the next week as the team return to action.

“Taking the four games Pocognoli has had, he's just come into the job, so a lot of information has been passed down to the players,” said Hutton. “Even with an extended break, which he would have appreciated, it's very difficult to get concepts across in such a short period of time. He'll be looking to develop that and reinforce his tactical ideas. Hopefully, they digest it better going into these two games.

“They beat North Macedonia away, so you'd hope he can get his first win at home to put that to bed. Switzerland away is going to be difficult, but you want to see progression in how they understand his philosophy on the pitch. It's still very early in his tenure and he's going to be given time to get it right. He's refreshed the squad with younger faces, and they need time to adapt as well, so while it has to improve, it requires patience.”

One of the main points of contention has been Scotland’s inability to finish chances that come their way. With Kieron Bowie the only striker to get on the scoresheet last month, questions have been asked about who should get the nod to lead the forward line in the upcoming games. Hutton believes one man has the number nine shirt - for now, at least.

“I know it's been an issue,” Hutton told OLBG. “Even going back to when I was playing, and that's no slight on anyone who played, but we lacked a guy who guarantees goals. Everything has been workmanlike, working hard and holding the ball up, but you need someone to put the ball in the back of the net.

“I think [Oli} McBurnie is the go-to guy at this moment. I really like Kieron Bowie and Robbie Ure, they're young and they will get better in the leagues they're in, improving technically and in their hold-up play. McBurnie is the main man right now, though the others will be breathing down his neck.”

#1940. Sky: Ramos involved but has minimal support – the numbers that illustrate Amorim’s point

Some interesting analysis on AC Milan and Goncalo Ramos’ attacking struggles has been provided by the Sky studios.

It was a familiar tale for Ramos during Milan’s 2-1 win over Genoa on Sunday. He was involved but rarely inside the box, then he was selfless instead of ruthless in front of goal when he chose to square for Christian Pulisic to make it 2-0.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

The worries are starting to grow regarding whether the Portuguese can provide the output required of a number nine that cost €70m. Yet, the Rossoneri have scored 23 goals in 11 league games which suggests goals are coming from elsewhere, sometimes with Ramos’ help.

Sky offered some interesting insight after Sunday’s game. Firstly, they picked out just how involved Ramos actually is with various aspects of Milan’s overall play.

For example, he is first among Serie A strikers for interceptions and recoveries, while he is second for receptions, touches and duels. He is third for passes.

He is first among centre-forwards in the league for touches in the middle third of the field and touches in the opposition half. He is second for fouls committed plus fouls suffered among forwards, with 41.

Sky then shift the focus to the team’s overall play to try and explain why Ramos perhaps isn’t getting the quality service and is having to drop deeper as a result.

They look at data per 30 minutes of possession. Milan are first in Serie A for build-up actions, but they are 20th for entries into the final third and entries into the opposition box.

Amorim’s side are 19th for percentage of touches in the attacking third and 18th in percentage of touches in the opposition box. With numbers like these, there isn’t much for Ramos to get on the end of.

What does this tell us? Well, Amorim’s post match assessment about struggling to get the ball from the defensive third into the final third are true. Milan have a lot of the ball but still struggle to progress it, as the coach told Sky.

“I think it’s difficult for a striker when he doesn’t score goals. But I’ll repeat: we don’t spend much time in the final third of the pitch. We have possession, we’re improving our ball output, but we’re missing that. When we’re consistently in the final third, Gonçalo will score a lot of goals,” he said.

“It’s a team problem, we’re not helping Ramos, but he’s helping us a lot. It’s a process, a journey. And we’re not yet at the point of being so dominant that Ramos spends most of his time in the opponent’s penalty area. We’re still a long way off.”

#1939. Powers of recovery on show from Eastbourne Borough – now for double knockout test

On Tuesday night, the Sports swept away visitors Dulwich Hamlet 4-2 - and so moved swiftly on, after themselves conceding four goals on Saturday. So what went wrong at Dartford?

Boss Steve King addressed that: "That was the worst that we've played under me. We were all over the place defensively. There were individual mistakes and collective errors.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

"We had our moments, had our chances - we hit the crossbar, hit the post. Josh Rees is about to score at the back post and he's having the shirt pulled off his back.

"But all in all, that first half performance was unacceptable. We chopped and changed a few things for the second half, but Dartford took their foot off the gas. You cannot concede four goals in a half of football."

Borough supporters - and many observers further afield - have frankly been raising their expectations week by week, as King's team chalked up the victories. But his post-match verdict was right on the money.

Firstly, Borough's defensive resources were stretched beyond the limit. And secondly, their errors were ruthlessly punished by an in-form Dartford. "There hasn't been another opponent that we've played who were as clinical as that.

"But listen, we've been on a heck of a run, fourteen wins out of fifteen. I said a few words, but nothing too strong. Pick yourselves up, and we go again!"

And go again they did: on a bleak Tuesday night, the Sports blew away visitors Dulwich Hamlet 4-2. With a relentless fixture schedule, King and his staff must manage resources.

At Dartford he had to field a centre-back pairing of full-back Elliott Johnson and the freshly returning Harry Phipps. And when Matthew Hayden - arguably the find of the season - chose the Dartford trip to have an off-day, the writing was on the dressing-room wall.

But with that game out of their systems, another three league points were in the kitty after Tuesday's victory.

King said of the Hamlet win: "At times we were very good. DIsappointed with the first Dulwich goal - it's a good finish but he's got in between our defenders. But then a good recovery from that with two excellent goals, from Josh (Rees) and Macca (Darren McQueen).

"At 3-1 I felt comfortable, but then we should have gone on to score more. Five, six, seven with the chances we were missing. At that point I actually said to Ryan (Northmore, assistant manager) - they're going to score again! And then it's going to be game on again!

"We were just woeful in our finishing! So that little period of the game wasn't great - and we've given Dulwich a leg up. But then Nashy Liam Nash) has scored and it's great to have him back!

"So it could have been much more comfortable. But when you lose a game (at Dartford) the question is - can you recover? And we have done that, and it's another win under the belt.

"The conditions were tough again with the wind and the rain - but it's another three points, and that's all you ever get for a victory. It's the most important thing. If you can get three points and play really well, that's even better. But the points are the first requirement.

"It was actually a tough night, because we've got some illness in the camp. And through the day we weren't quite sure who was ill and who had recovered, and who was fit and who was still injured.

"We were just counting the bodies. Gold (Omotayo) was ill and Terrell (Egbri) was ill. Elliott (Johnson) had a shoulder that swelled up. Fortunately we've had a good bench and so they all played their part. But it was a challenging day, with a lot of permutations!

Now Borough can turn their attention to a different competition - or two, in fact.

Tomorrow (Saturday) Chertsey Town visit the Connect Management Stadium in the FA Trophy. The Curfews play in the Southern League Premier South.

This Borough squad is full of seasoned professionals, and - in contrast to recent seasons - completely free of would-be superstars. They work hard, they know the system, and - most of all - they have brought a little bit of joy back. There is a cheerful connection with Borough's ever so slightly barmy army of supporters - who sang their hearts out, even in defeat, at Dartford.

King said: "Now we turn to Saturday, and Chertsey in the Trophy. Chertsey Town are a good side - they've beaten some strong opposition this season, and they've won again in midweek. So I'm expecting a very tough game.

"It's the Trophy of course, and a break from the league, which is actually welcome. And then another cup game next Tuesday (Littlehampton in the Sussex Senior Cup). So they are coming thick and fast - we will have had six weeks of Saturday-Tuesday-Saturday. I'm hoping by Saturday week to have players back and to be closer to a full squad - when we make the trip to Enfield for a really important league game!"

As King said, Tuesday sees yet another home fixture, the Sports welcoming Littlehampton Town in the Senior Cup.

Two seasons ago, the Marigolds muscled Borough out of a Senior Cup semi-final at Lancing. Revenge? Not exactly, but a chance to set the record straight, and score a few more goals. It's never goalless at the Lane.

#1938. Inside big Andy Robertson decision as Scotland landmark brings Liverpool legend comeback quip

Andy Robertson stands on the brink of making international history in the coming days as he prepares to move level with Sir Kenny Dalglish’s appearance record for Scotland.

The Tottenham full-back is closing in on a significant career milestone that would see him match Dalglish on 102 caps for his country should he feature in Friday’s UEFA Nations League clash against North Macedonia at Hampden, underlining his importance to the team over the past decade.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Since making his senior international debut back in 2014, the 32-year-old has gone to captain his nation and help guide Scotland to successive European Championship tournaments.

His longevity and consistency at the highest level have made him a central figure in the national team, with former Scotland manager Alex McLeish among those who have witnessed first-hand the qualities that make Robertson such an important leader.

McLeish handed Robertson the armband in 2018 and believes his standing in the Premier League, alongside his personality and popularity within the dressing room, made his decision a straightforward one as he paid a glowing tribute to the defender.

“He's been an amazing servant for club and country,” McLeish declared just over a month on from presenting Robertson with a framed shirt to commemorate earning his 100th cap. “Andy's obviously on the verge of equalling Kenny's caps record so maybe Kenny will need to make a comeback! No, seriously Andy is still doing the country proud and it's great to see.

“When I made him captain it felt like natural progress. I just felt that his stature, as a player at Liverpool, playing at the level he was playing at, made him the ideal man. He has a real passion for the game and he's also super popular with the other players. They all respect him and look up to him.”

Moving level with Dalglish’s tally in the all-time charts would represent another major landmark in a career that has seen Robertson become one of the most successful Scottish footballers of his generation and cement his place among the country's greatest ever servants.

Meanwhile, another former Scotland boss, Craig Levein, has urged patience when assessing the early stages of Sebastien Pocognoli's tenure, suggesting it remains too soon to make firm judgements about the new head coach.

With Scotland entering a new chapter following Steve Clarke's time in charge, Levein believes there will inevitably be a transition period under the Belgian as some of the more experienced heads approach the latter stages of their international careers.

“It's too early to tell, isn't it? At some point, some of these players who are getting on a little bit are going to be getting into the point where they would probably be coming off the bench and then maybe disappearing from the squads altogether,” Levein admitted.

“Steve did an unbelievable job in getting Scotland to these tournaments. I do think that he had probably the best squad of players that Scotland had for a long, long time. Those two things merged very well, and they did a fantastic job.

“I don't know much about the new guy at all. I haven't really needed to do any research like you guys have. So we'll just have to give the guy time and wait and see what happens.”

On another afternoon it could have finished 6-1 to Borough, but they scored four from five shots on target and we managed one from ten. Sometimes football leaves you wondering how on earth you have lost a game like that.

Our fans, however, were amazing. You sang and sang, even when there was no way back. When you have travelled to support your team and the afternoon goes against you, that takes some doing. Thank you.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

I did wonder whether the manager of the month curse had struck again! Congratulations to Steve King on his thoroughly deserved award. One difficult afternoon certainly doesn’t undo the work that earned it.

What mattered next was how the boys responded, and Tuesday evening against Dulwich Hamlet gave us plenty to be proud of.

Conceding in the second minute was hardly the start we wanted. After Saturday, it would have been easy for heads to drop. Instead, these boys worked their socks off and went into half-time 3-1 up.

The second half was harder going in the rain, but the boys stuck at it and came away with a 4-2 win. A proper response to Saturday and three very welcome points, especially as Welling dropped a couple of points down the road.

Bobby, our commentator, and I both had Liam Nash as our man of the match. Considering he has been out for so many weeks, he was amazing. It was lovely to see him back playing so well.

It was bitterly cold, too. To everyone who came out, wrapped up and got behind the team, thank you. There are certainly warmer ways to spend a Tuesday evening, and we appreciate you choosing to spend yours with us.

Tomorrow is a huge occasion as Chertsey Town visit for an FA Trophy second round tie. I would love to see a big crowd at Priory Lane helping the boys take another step in the competition. Bring a friend, bring the family and bring your voices. A few extra layers might be sensible as well!

We have also had another trophy to celebrate. Our Spirit of Football team recently paraded their first silverware in front of a packed stadium, and we are so proud of every one of them. Seeing the reception they received was a lovely moment for everyone involved.

As the weather gets more miserable, there is plenty happening indoors at the club. Padel is great fun for all ages, good exercise and, judging by everyone who has tried it, highly addictive. Come down and give it a go.

Our new simulators also let you play golf at thousands of courses, with all the excitement and no wet clothes afterwards. Both the Padel Centre and Simulator Centre make great Christmas party venues, whether you are getting together with friends, family or work colleagues.

For now, though, let’s get behind the boys tomorrow and make it another cup afternoon to remember.

#1936. What channel is Scotland v North Macedonia? TV and live stream for Nations League clash

Sebastien Pocognoli begins his second international break as Scotland head coach against North Macedonia at Hampden on Friday.

The Nations League fixture will provide the Belgian with a chance to claim his first home victory at the third attempt after the disappointing defeats by Switzerland and Slovenia last month.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

North Macedonia meanwhile are searching for a sharp turnaround after losing five consecutive matches and failing to score in their last eight games, including the 2-0 defeat by Scotland in Skopje last month.

Pocognoli has endured an underwhelming start to his Scotland tenure, collecting just four points from his opening four games to leave his side third in Nations League Group B1 and facing an uphill task to finish in the top two.

Switzerland top the table on the maximum 12 points meaning Scotland are no longer able to overtake them or secure automatic promotion to Nations League A. A runners-up finish is still possible, which would secure a promotion play-off against a team who finishes second bottom of a Group A section, but would require Scotland to overhaul Slovenia, who are three points ahead in second place in the table.

A top two finish in Group B1 is also required for Scotland to guarantee second seed status for the Euro 2028 qualifying draw, which takes place on December 6. Otherwise, Scotland are almost certain to be a pot three team.

Because the Slovenians hold the head-to-head advantage, Scotland must finish ahead of them on points to overtake them. Slovenia host Switzerland on Friday before travelling to Skopje to face North Macedonia on Monday. A victory in either match will clinch second place for them.

After Scotland host North Macedonia on Friday they travel to St. Gallen to face Switzerland on Monday. Pocognoli’s men will need four points if Slovenia lose both matches, but will need the maximum six points if Slovenia pick up one or two points.

The Nations League Group B1 fixture between Scotland and North Macedonia takes place at Hampden Park, Glasgow, on Friday, November 13, 2026. Kick-off is 7.45pm.

The match will be broadcast live on BBC2 and the BBC Scotland channel with coverage starting at 7.30pm.

The match will be available to live stream on the BBC Sport website and the BBC iPlayer.

Sebastien Pocognoli has been boosted by the return from injury of Kieran Tierney, Scott McTominay and Che Adams with the trio all in contention to start. However, the Scotland head coach has suffered a triple blow in defence, losing three centre-backs who started for him last month with the withdrawals of Stephen Welsh and Luis Binks adding to the absence of Scott McKenna from the original squad.

You can view our predicted starting XI here.

Slovak referee Michal Očenáš has been appointed to officiate the match at Hampden. He will be joined by an all-Slovakian on-field officiating team, featuring Adam Jekkel and Tobiáš Pacák as assistant referees, alongside Boris Marhefka serving as the fourth official.

UEFA has assigned an Austrian pairing to the VAR booth. Alan Kijas will act as the Video Assistant Referee (VAR) for the fixture, while Harald Lechner will support him as the Assistant Video Assistant Referee (AVAR).

#1932. Tottenham wonderkid and £16m Everton star on Scotland radar as Sebastien Pocognoli confirms approach

Sebastien Pocognoli has revealed he has made approaches to Tottenham youngster Archie Gray and Everton midfielder Hayden Hackney about representing Scotland as he looks to strengthen his international options.

The Belgian head coach is determined to identify talented players with Scottish connections who could potentially represent the national team, and has confirmed that both Premier League prospects feature on his recruitment radar.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Gray and Hackney have represented England at youth level but are eligible to play for Scotland, although neither has committed to switching their international allegiance. Pocognoli admits he has already established contact with the pair but insists any decision will ultimately have to come from the players themselves.

His predecessor, Steve Clarke, previously attempted to persuade the likes of Elliot Anderson and Harvey Barnes to represent Scotland, without success. However, the country has enjoyed greater luck in other cases, with Scott McTominay and Che Adams going on to become influential figures after opting to play for the Tartan Army.

Pocognoli is currently satisfied with the depth available to him as Scotland prepare for their final Nations League fixtures against North Macedonia and Switzerland. Nevertheless, he believes expanding the pool of eligible talent must remain an ongoing priority.

Speaking about his efforts to identify potential recruits, Pocognoli said: “I am busy with everything. We know which players are eligible to represent the country one day. It’s won't come from me, it has to come from them to show it. I try to anticipate everything. The best way is to be proactive and creative in certain situations.

“The depth of the squad is already big without these other names. I’m very happy with it because we have a good double-up and triple-up in each position. But it’s part of my role, for sure [to find players]. Not only for me but for other people working at the Scottish FA. We are on it. We also have a lot of good players in the Under-21s and that’s the first step for me, for the future.

“But yeah, I have had direct or indirect contact (with Gray and Hackney). When I go to the direct contact it’s because I feel it’s a first positive approach. So yeah, I’ve done it with many players. I’ll do my best to bring them.”

Gray and Hackney have different international backgrounds, with Pocognoli acknowledging that any potential switch would require patience.

Gray, the son of former Scotland striker Andy Gray, also has family links to Scottish football through Leeds United legends Frank and Eddie Gray, both of whom represented the national side. The Tottenham midfielder has featured for England at every youth level but has yet to make his senior debut.

Hackney, meanwhile, previously represented Scotland at Under-21 level before switching his international allegiance to England.

Pocognoli believes the age of the two players makes them particularly interesting prospects but insists there is no immediate pressure for either to make a decision.

“With Barnes it was different. I knew before my first camp that he was different,” he said. “The two other lads [Gray and Hackney] are young lads. It’s a long way [away]. But if you wait too long, it might not be the right moment. In a year’s time, we will see. Right now, we have players in the squad who are performing well.

“It will always be up to them [current players] to be the priority, because we’ve built things and we’ve had time with the ones who are here right now. But we are on it. We are always proactive in all of these situations. What is very exciting about those two names is that they are young players.

“That’s interesting. We have to look and manage the situation. But it won’t be a definitive choice from them - because we weren’t proactive. That has to be clear. We are proactive.

“The best way to convince players is to show good football, show them they can come to us, enjoy it and be successful. They have to feel when they leave a top club that they arrive here into top conditions and a top environment.

“That’s the best publicity we can offer, to show good football. Yeah [McTominay is an example] but there are many.”

#1931. ‘Ahead of where we thought we’d be’ – Dolan says home defeats won’t derail Hastings United

United went down 3-0 to Sevenoaks on Tuesday night, soon after home reverses to Faversham and Deal. It was a setback after a fine 3-0 win at Cray Valley PM had put them back on top of the Isthmian South East table.

Dolan insists it’s still been a great start to the season and they’re ahead of where they expected to be. And he’s ready to try to get them back to their best home form against Steyning tomorrow.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

"Sevenoaks are another very good team – they move the ball well and work hard as a team – they’re very athletic and quick on the counter.

"We weren’t really at the races. As much as we were battling we weren’t really hurting them like we should have done or how we know we can. That’s something we’re looking to rectify.

"The red card didn’t have a big effect on the game, I don’t think. We’ll never know if having 11 men would have kept us in the game til the end and got us a point or something out of the game. We can’t do much about that.

"There wasn’t much in it to be a red card but it’s two yellows and that’s the way it is in football these days – you have to be very careful.

"But our performance wasn’t ‘at it’ – and that’s maybe down to a lot of games in short space of time. I think in the past couple of months we’ve only had one week where we haven’t had a Tuesday game. We’ve played a lot of games in a short space of time, as has everyone, but I think we’re running on a slightly smaller squad, though a very good squad.

"That’s always going to take its toll at some point. It’s now a case of can we freshen it, can we build on it, can we look to add one or two to freshen the squad up a little and see what we can do from there. We’ve got another Saturday-Tuesday this week and there’s a lot of football to play in the season.

"We’ve come through this period doing okay – we’re okay in the league, we have a lot of points on the board considering we’re a very yojng squad and we’ve rebuilt in the summer. I think we’re ahead of where we expected to be so all in all I’m pretty happy – it’s just a case of can we add to it and try to find more consistency as a team.”

Asked if home form dip could be down to nerves he said he didn’t. “I think it’s a blip that we’ll get over. We started off so well at home this season and it’s now a case of can we freshen it up a little, whether that’s bringing players in or rotating players we have in the squad already and trying to find the right formula at home again – whether that’s changing shape or changing personnel.

"We’ll look into those things as a management but I do think everyone during a season knows you’re not going to win every home. It’s not ideal losing three home games in a row so we’ll look at it. Whoever can keep that consistency through the season will do well. Having a young and newly built squad, it’s hard to get that consistency.

"It’ll take a bit of time but we’re ahead of where we wanted to be this season. I’m pretty pleased and we’ll see how we go from here.”

Three days earlier it was a 3-0 win at Cray Valley PM courtesy of goals by Kes Clarke, Warren Mfula and Sam Pidgeon.

Dolan said: “Iit was a good win. I wouldn’t say we were on top from the word go. They created quite a few opportunities first half which ex expcted, because they’re a good team with very good players in attacking areas.

"We expected them to come at us and, being at home, to creat opportunities, which they did. But unfortunately for them, they didn’t take them – and when we created our own chances, we did and we punished them.

"I keep saying to our boys, when we get opportunities we have to punish teams.Normally we get punished so it was nice for us to be on the other side of it, punishing a team for not taking their chances.

"The second half we dominated – I think they only had one shot in the half and it was a fairly comfortable save for Harry. So it was a good away win and good performance all round.

It’s Steyning next at the Pilot Field and Dolan said: “Every game is tricky – every opposition team have their own threats and can cause you problems. We have to concentrate on how we deal with that and get on the front foot, and can we create and take chances. I genuinely think that if we go back to what we were doing at the start of the season, particularly at home, teams won’t be able to deal with us. We’ve got to find that consistency.

"Steyning we will give the respect they deserve. We’ll have trained hard and gone over a few things but we expect a tough game. Every game in this league. We aim to go into Saturday and look to rectify Tuesday.

"Then we have Whitehawk in the senior cup. You want to win every game, whether it’s a cup or league match. And with the final being at the Amex, it would be amazing to get there. If we win it’s happy days but if we fall short yet we’ve turned up and put in a performance but luck isn’t on our side, that’s fair enough. But we want to win it."

#1929. Sheffield Wednesday opt out as reason Dave Challinor picked his battles made clear

Trying to lift rather than turn the fortunes of the League One club, he is doing so with one hand tied behind his back. Rightly or wrongly, it is why he decided not to risk making the situation worse on Wednesday.

Already in the last 32 of the Football League Trophy, all that was at stake was whether they or Accrington Stanley would top the group and secure a home tie. The League Two club wanted it more. Far more.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Whilst they named a strong side, Challinor basically wrote the game off, more interested in protecting his first-teamers from injury than using what was effectively the second of two pre-season games for him to decide his line-up for his first match that really matters – Plymouth Argyle at home on Saturday.

So it was no surprise Accrington ran out 4-0 winners, Josh Smith's goal added to by the Charlies – Brown, Warren and Caton.

When the final whistle blew, it felt like a missed opportunity to get a first win since the 5-0 hammering of Wimbledon in mid-October.

But when Challinor revealed another key player is now injured, it made a little bit more sense.

With eight of the midweek XI having only kicked off 14 league matches for the Owls – the other three only had a combined 75 – Challinor's teamsheet was an act of surrender. Picking your battles, he would say.

Louis Poland and substitute James Kay made debuts, and there was a first start to Denny Oliver.

Connal Trueman made some saves to put minds at rest if Joe Lumley is not fit on Saturday – that seems touch and go –and Oliver and winger Samuel Duruh showed flashes, but no one cast doubt on Challinor's best team, even with all the injuries.

Striker George Brown's first outing of an injury-hit 2026 was a fillip, but after 45 minutes of a fairly dead Trophy game, not a solution.

"It's not been that useful," said Challinor, in reference to the results when asked how helpful starting with two cup games was, "but it's given us a chance to see people.

"We wanted to progress on Sunday (in the FA Cup first round but) we were probably not going to win the FA Cup this season and we're definitely not going to win it now.

"We used it to look at things, but also try and protect some players. That didn't work in some instances. Progression in the (Trophy) allowed us to prioritise Saturday.

"I suppose (Wednesday's game was) what I expected, really.

"Some young players made their debuts and it was a really proud moment for them. They should be better for the experience whether it's good or bad."

The game felt like an obligation to tick off on a freezing night when only 5,472 supporters were in attendance. Fans can be cold on the Trophy, defiled by Premier League under-21 teams, at the best of times. Some take a club of Wednesday's stature having to field their first team in it as an insult.

Depending who they select at the weekend, the Owls could be fined for Wednesday’s weak team. Even if their mitigation does not wash, the punishment will be small, £5,000, but this is a club forced to count the pennies as it emerges from the wreckage left by Dejphon Chansiri.

So what was Challinor protecting them from?

"We've got six or seven players out," he said. "We've got four on international duty. We're coming into a run of fixtures between now and the new year of 11 games so we're going to need all of our players."

Liam Cooper, Billy Mitchell and Louis Barry had trained at the start of the week but not risked. Erine Weaver was.

"Ernie is struggling on the back of the foot injury he had last season," revealed Challinor.

"He's probably got into a rhythm where he plays games and then misses a few days' training to let his foot settle down a bit.

"I thought in the second half he did really well apart from the one mistake where he jumped in and then we concede the (third) goal as a consequence."

Oldham Athletic winning after extra-time on Sunday took a toll.

"Dish (Di'Shon Bernard) was like a tin man on Monday, Tuesday," said his manager. "Jammer (Jamal Lowe), Davo (Davis Keillor-Dunn) had a bit of cramp, Yan (Valery) came off with some cramp. Ash (Maynard-Brewer) got a bit of a whack. He's fine, he probably misses the weekend."

"Max (Lowe) has got a recurrence of the injury he had earlier in the season, so he's going to be out for probably four to six weeks."

Left-sided defender is a key player, especially with Reece James out too.

"It’s disappointing because you saw the impact and profile of him in terms of what we want to try and do in possession,” added Challinor, "but something we'll have to deal with."

So was a proud club surrendering a game, even one of this low priority.

Now Challinor needs Saturday’s end to justify the means.

#1928. Seven Brighton stars out of contract this summer - including latest Chelsea transfer target

Brighton have big contract decisions to make on key players between now and the end of the season.

The Seagulls are flying high in the Premier League as last Sunday's 2-0 home win against Brentford took them second in the table.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

Fabian Hurzeler's team are also juggling the demands of the Uefa Conference League as they sit fifth in Europe's third tier competition and on track to qualify for the knockout stage.

It's been an impressive start for the Seagulls and the latest international break will now doubt give them a chance to reflect on the season so far and plan for the next stage of the campaign.

Brighton's decision makers will also be well aware that a number of their key men are out of contract this summer.

Jason Steele: The England squad goalkeeper and Brighton No 2 is out of contract this summer. The 36-year-old joined Brighton in 2018 from Sunderland and has made 65 appearances for the Seagulls with 25 clean sheets. Hurzeler previously described Steele as the best No 2 in the Premier League.

Tom McGill: The 26-year-old No 3 goalkeeper joined Brighton in 2014 and has progressed through the youth ranks. The Canadian born stopper is yet to make a first team appearance for Brighton and has had loans at Worthing, Greenwich, Basingstoke, Crawley Town and Milton Keynes. He's been called up to the senior Canada national team multiple times but is yet to feature. He may wish to leave this summer in search of regular football.

Lewis Dunk: The 34-year-old skipper has started the season superbly and helped Brighton to seven clean sheets in the Premier League this term. He's made 533 appearances for Brighton and I'd be amazed if he doesn't get another deal this summer

Yasin Ayari: Here's an interesting situation. The club and player are yet to agree on a new contract but it is believed Brighton do have the option of a further year for the Sweden international. He's been brilliant in the midfield for past few season and the BBC recently reported that "Brighton's best customer" Chelsea are keen on the 23-year-old.

Pascal Gross: The 35-year-old has started every match in all competitions so far this season. He's an absolute class act on and off the pitch and if he doesn't deserve a new contract, then I'm not sure who does!

Kaoru Mitoma: Is this the summer Brighton say goodbye to their Japan international. The 29-year-old is yet to feature this season as he recovers from a hamstring injury. He's due to return soon after the international break and much will depend on how he performs in the second half of the season. If he's fully fit and firing, Mitoma remains one of the most dangerous wingers in the Premier League.

Promise David: The Canadian international joined on loan from Union SG and the Seagulls are believed to have an option to buy this summer for around £20m, if they wish to do so. He's made two late substitute appearances in the Premier League against Leeds and Chelsea. Yet to impress.

#1925. Ordine reveals Amorim’s substitution vs. Genoa that sent ‘a message to the owners’

Franco Ordine believes that Ruben Amorim’s changes in the game against Genoa served as a message to his superiors.

Milan went into yesterday’s match having lost against Ferencvaros in a Europa League game that once again showed the limitations of the team when rotated. The task of effectively managing work loads is not made easier by the list of injuries.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Pietro Terracciano, Matteo Gabbia, Fikayo Tomori, Alexis Saelemaekers, Ruben Loftus-Cheek, Samuel Chukwueze and Strahinja Pavlovic were all out for the match at the Stadio Luigi Ferraris, with the Serbian centre-back being the latest to enter the treatment room.

In today’s edition of Corriere dello Sport (via MilanNews), Ordine analysed Milan’s win at the Marassi. He spoke about how the injury situation has forced Amorim to make certain choices, ones that lay everything bare in view of a potentially important winter transfer window.

“Having also lost Pavlovic, who is one of the most consistent players and the most ‘applied’ in training, they had to improvise Diawara at centre-back and even Musah at left-back,” he said.

“And for those who say the lack of confidence in Estupiñan on this occasion was deserved (he came on with just minutes to go and managed to provoke a free kick at the end of injury time that could have proved fatal), some explanation for the failure to use Bartesaghi would be worth seeking.

“Not only that. Later on, when it became clear that the fatigue accumulated on Thursday against the Hungarians had crushed Milan in the final 20-30 metres, Terracciano emerged from the bench as second centre-back on the left, a right-footed player who has only had a few poor performances so far.

“This is essentially a message to the owners, who have already promised to intervene in the January transfer window to fill the gaps. The point is precisely this: until then, the Portuguese coach must continue with his current strength.

“Of course, after the break, he may be able to recover some of the injured players (Tomori, Pavlovic, Loftus Cheek, perhaps Gabbia), but certainly not Saelemakers and Chekwueze, who will be ready between February and March.

“For this reason, the strengthening plan must unravel another knot that has remained tangled for now: that of Ramos’s deputy. The Portuguese, who yesterday drew applause for his generous assist to Pulisic in the penalty area, seems doomed to play every game, and to the very end, because Camarda is only called upon in rare circumstances.

“Here too, as in the case of Estupiñan, who was not sold, acknowledging the error of judgment made in the summer is a sign of intelligence!”

“I was a bit unlucky after the Villa game,” Hinshelwood said to the Albion website.

Brighton have enjoyed a fine start to the season and last Sunday’s 2-0 win against Brentford moved them second in the table.

Brighton - along with the rest of the Premier League - are currently paused for the international break and resume action on November 22 at Hull City.

Hinshelwood added: “The boys were in great form and still are, so that made it a little bit easier during the tough time. Now I’m just trying to come back, support the team, and get back in the starting line-up.

“They’re doing so well, so I’m pushing for every opportunity I get to try and do my best to help the team move forward.”

Hinshelwood is known for his versatility but of late he has impressed in the No 10 role. He added: “I'll play anywhere the manager needs or wants me to play, but I'm really enjoying the higher position. I think I can contribute with goals and assists.

“When I first came through, I was playing full-back all the time, and I thought that was going to be me for the rest of my career.

“Last season, I had a good run in the ten role, and the manager obviously trusts me and likes me to play there.”

Scotland held onto their lead, given to them after McGinn drove into the box following strong centre-forward play from Che Adams, for the best part of three minutes.

A penalty, awarded after a VAR check a good couple of minutes after goalkeeper Stole Dimitrievski's trip on Ben Gannon-Doak occurred, saved Scotland’s blushes with 16 minutes left and kept their Nations League hopes just about alive.

McGinn did the necessary from the spot although Oli McBurnie, who had replaced Adams six minutes earlier, might have appreciated being given the ball in his seemingly eternal quest for an international goal. It was perhaps too important a kick to take any chances. A manager’s future prospects might have rested on it.

It was a case of third time lucky for Pocognoli as he secured his first Hampden win on what had not seemed like a particularly auspicious date. For the first time since the notorious 0-0 draw against Uruguay that torpedoed their 1986 World Cup, Scotland were in action on a Friday the 13th. What could possibly go wrong? A lot, it seemed at times.

If anything underlined that these are very different times for Scotland it was the sight of Scott McTominay, almost a year to the day since that overhead kick against Denmark, launching himself into the air again in an effort to meet Gilmour’s cross. Although he connected well, the direction was lacking. The ball went high over the bar.

There was no goal from the halfway line this time either. Instead, we were treated to one of the worst misses ever seen at Hampden when Gilmour skied the ball from seven yards seconds after the interval.

The Hampden crowd was getting testy. Boos had greeted the half-time whistle, with the score still goalless and the hosts perhaps lucky not to have conceded.

McGinn’s opener ten minutes after half-time seemed like just the medicine. However, underlining how this was never straightforward, Macedonia equalised almost immediately. They had to score a goal sometime but it was not a good look for Scotland or McTominay, who was beaten in the air at the front post by Elmin Rastodar following a corner.

A clumsy challenge at the other end by Dimitrievski on Gannon-Doak, whose poor touch had already looked to have taken the chance away from him, gave Scotland the gratifying chance to equalise from the spot 17 minutes later.

The hosts had endured an uncertain start that was a decent indicator of what lay ahead. What seemed like teething problems might have been attributed to a defence playing together for the first time. Ryan Porteous was brought back into the starting line-up, his first start since the opening match of Euro 2024 when he was sent off.

Luke Graham, meanwhile, earned his second cap - a first start for Scotland - and was planted right in the middle of the three-man backline. After surviving a few shaky moments initially, the Stoke City defender acquitted himself superbly well.

North Macedonia’s dismal run, which included not having scored in this Nations League campaign so far, perhaps convinced Pocognoli he could make such alterations though injury had restricted his options. Poertoeus, though, hadn’t even been named in the original squad.

Defence wasn’t expected to be an issue. It was a Friday night after a long week at work. Fans wanted to be entertained, they wanted to see some tangible evidence of a new Scotland they have been promised. Pocognoli might wear a suit very well but he’s not proved himself to be his predecessor’s equal at obtaining results, although this was more like it. The fear is that this supposedly more free-flowing Scotland has made them blunter. The phrase the emperor’s new clothes could not be banished from the mind.

Not even McTominay could ignite things. He seemed ready to burst the net just a few minutes later after Lewis Ferguson’s header found the Napoli midfielder with his back to goal in the box. When he turned, it looked like there would be only one outcome. However, Dimitrievski made a tremendous save low to his left.

Yes, this was another occasion where the North Macedonian goalkeeper excelled himself, just as he did in Skopje at the start of last month.

Another save, when he plucked a deflected Adams header out from beneath his crossbar, was even better. There were mitigating factors for Scotland failing to make the breakthrough in the opening half.

It might have been worse for the home team. A cute lay-off from Darko Churlinov set up skipper Enis Bardhi, who lashed a left-footed shot into the side-netting. Most of the Hampden crowd feared the ball had gone in. The smattering of North Macedonia fans were beside themselves.

Sadly for them, happily for the vast majority, the rippling effect was due to the ball hitting the wrong side of the net. It might have been marginally offside in any case. Jeers greeted the blowing of the half-time whistle moments later, nonetheless.

Would Scotland come out with a renewed sense of purpose? It seemed so. Adams pounced on a short pass back and cut the ball back while Dimitrievski dithered.

Billy Gilmour is no one’s idea of a prolific goalscorer but even he couldn’t miss from seven yards, goal gaping. He did. Quite incredibly, the ball comfortably cleared the bar. People were referencing Chris Iwelumo, meaning it was one of the worst misses of all time. It was at the right end, certainly. McGinn showed him how to do it, moving level with Hughie Gallacher in third place on 24 goals in the all-time list of goalscorers and ensuring Andy Robertson’s record-equalling 102nd cap would also be the victorious one the skipper deserved.

#1922. Why Steve McClaren's bad experiences can be good for Rotherham United's Alex Bruce

At other clubs, Bruce might have been shown the door by now, with the Millers only above the League Two trapdoor on goals scored, having played a game more than 23rd-placed Colchester United.

But his fate is effectively in the hands of McClaren, owner Tony Stewart's sounding board.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

The York-born former England manager knows the scale of upheaval at the New York Stadium this summer, and also the value of a bit of patience.

He lost his first four matches as a manager in 2001, and ended the year with Middlesbrough only out of the Premier League relegation zone on goal difference, yet left as their most successful boss.

"I've been through this so many times and if you want a career in management, get used to it," he says. "It doesn't go away.

"Very few times I've been into a football club and it's been easy the first three months. It's not.

"We see that in politics. The first 100 days are difficult.

"He (Bruce) is lucky he's got good experience around him to tell him to shut up moaning in your messages to the players. That's the message to the players – shut up whingeing.

"I've kind of got to be the truth teller to say that's no excuse, we should be doing that better."

And in a different way, he has to be Stewart's truth-teller too.

"I said to him, when you're at the top, you have to be the calm one," says McClaren. "Under the water you might be flapping but it's staying calm and composed, having a plan, sticking to the plan and making sure you fulfil it.

"In the meantime get through the bad times as best you can, stick together and believe in your own ability.”

‘When you have the answer, you can call me every day,’ the Reds head coach replied when The Yorkshire Post tabled the question.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

The Reds shipped two goals apiece after the interval in both games. While the 5-2 and 7-2 scorelines didn't take too much gloss off the wins, the pattern remains a tad annoying.

It continued a worrying trend. The last eight goals that Barnsley have conceded in cup matches have all arrived following the break.

While their recent concessions did not cost them, the story is different at league level, which helps explain Barnsley's position in League One.

Ahead of Saturday’s crunch trip to fellow strugglers Wigan Athletic, the Reds sit second-from-bottom, with their hosts occupying the final spot in the relegation zone.

Barnsley have let in a creditable six goals in the first half of league games in 2026-27. The figure almost triples on the resumption.

The Reds' goal has been breached 16 times in the second period – only Bromley (17) has a worse third-tier record.

Stendel, inset, who is hopeful that the narrative changes with more plentiful options at his disposal in comparison to earlier this autumn said: "I know that we have conceded more in the second half.

“It's not only the defence, it's also the offence. Maybe in the past, we played five games in a row and played with a similar squad in every game. Maybe that’s a reason for it.

"Why can't we do it in the second half when we can do it in the first half? I think fitness is not a problem. I think we're one of the fittest teams in this league.

"I can see it every week in training. It's key that we defend for 90 minutes like most of the time in the first half. When we do it, I think we have a big chance to win a lot of games."

Relative defensive inexperience at this level – which will hopefully improve sooner rather than later – and lapses in concentration are two obvious reasons explaining this.

In what could well be a tense afternoon in Lancashire on Saturday, staying strong for the entire game could prove the difference.

In the EFL Cup tie between these two Roses rivals in August, Barnsley did that in fairness, scoring an equaliser in the final quarter, courtesy of Cameron McGeehan, before progressing on penalties.

A key late goal in their favour on Saturday could be far more important in terms of their season’s narrative.

Stendel added: "It’s more pressure maybe than in our situation normally, but it doesn't matter, it's one game.

"Pressure is part of football, but we need also a little bit of calm to play our game. We're looking forward to it. We're in good shape and in a positive momentum."

#1918. Sarina Wiegman receives honorary damehood from Prince William at Windsor Castle - after leading Lionesses to back-to-back European titles

Published: 14:28 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 19:04 EST, 10 November 2026

Lionesses manager Sarina Wiegman has been awarded an honorary damehood by Prince William after leading England to back-to-back Euro wins.

Wiegman is Dutch and therefore cannot be made a substantive dame. Instead she has picked up the honorary title, because the Netherlands does not have a British monarch as its head of state.

She said upon being awarded the title at Windsor Castle on Tuesday: 'I feel very privileged to receive my honorary Damehood from His Royal Highness The Prince of Wales at Windsor Castle today.

'It is a day I will never forget and made even more special by sharing it with members of my family.

'I would like to again express my sincere gratitude for this honour and for the continued respect and warmth I experience from the English people. I thank everyone for their support.'

Wiegman was named in the King's New Year's Honours list at the end of 2025, alongside several members of her England team.

England manager Sarina Wiegman (left) has been awarded an honourary damehood by Prince William (right)

Captain Leah Williamson was awarded a CBE, with Alex Greenwood, Keira Walsh, Georgia Stanway and Ella Toone all being honoured with MBEs.

Wiegman said at the time: 'I would like to express my sincere gratitude for this honour. When I first arrived in England, I could never have imagined the respect and warmth I've experienced from the English people. I deeply thank the fans for their support.

'This title is a reflection of my exceptional team of players and staff. My congratulations go to Alex, Ella, Georgia, Keira, Leah and also Dr Ritan Mehta who have all been celebrated for their brilliant contributions.

'Our team values mean that when there is recognition for one, then there is recognition for all. I want to pay tribute to every member of our EURO squad. They should all be celebrated for everything they brought to the pitch and for the positive role they play in society. I'm proud to work alongside such a dedicated group of people.'

The former Netherlands coach took over the England team in 2021 and led them to success at Euro 2022 and Euro 2025.

She also reached the World Cup final in 2023, and signed a new two-year contract extension earlier this year, which will take her to the end of the 2029 Euros.

Here's the latest on Vuskovic and a seven other Brighton stars - including head coach Fabian Hurzeler - who are attracting transfer interest.

Luka Vuskovic: Brighton smashed their transfer record to sign the Croatian teenager from Tottenham for just under £50m last summer. Vuskovic has been superb in the early stages of his Brighton career and the BBC reported today that Liverpool are keen. The 23-year-old, speaking ahead of Albion's Conference League win in Getafe, said: "You never know what will happen in future, but I'm happy at Brighton."

Yasin Ayari: The Sweden international and Brighton have so far failed to agree on a new contract. Yankuba Minteh: The flying Gambian is just getting back to full fitness after a leg injury. Liverpool made two bids of around £60m and £70m for the former Newcastle man last summer, which Brighton rejected. Minteh will have to prove his form and fitness in the second half the season and if he does, then expect further interest from Liverpool and perhaps other top clubs from the Premier League and across Europe.

Kaoru Mitoma: The Japan international is yet to feature this term as he recovers from a long term hamstring injury. The winger joined Brighton in 2021 for around £3m and proved himself to be one of the most dangerous wingers in the Premier League. The 29-year-old is out of contract this summer and could eye a move away if the offer is right. Many Brighton fans would be sorry to see him go. A unique talent.

Charalampos Kostoulas: The Greek teenager has made a huge impact this season with five goals and four assists in all competitions. Kostoulas joined Brighton in 2025 for around £30m and after a slow start, he's really started to find his form. His workrate is impressive, his finishing can be clinical and he's also capable of the spectacular. This week former England and Manchester United striker Teddy Sheringham was singing his praises and urged his former club Man United to sign him this summer.

Maxim De Cuyper: The Belgian international has perhaps been a surprise package this season. The left sided player has excelled in Mitoma's absence with four goals and four assists already this term. Brighton signed him for around £15m in 2025 and recent reports suggest Italian clubs Roma, AC Milan and Juventus are all keen, with a potential value of £60m.

Fabian Hurzeler: This adds another dynamic as the impressive young German head coach will no doubt be in high demand this summer. The 33-year-old has been hugely impressive for the Seagulls since arriving from St Pauli in 2024. Manchester United were previously linked with Hurzeler, who is now one of the most sought after young coaches in European football. He is under contract until June 2029 and Brighton will demand a hefty compensation package if a club tries to prise him away.

#1915. Mali vs Rwanda - prediction, team news, lineups

By Nsidibe Akpan | 11 Nov 2026 23:07, Last updated: 12 Nov 2026 18:01

Mali host Rwanda at the Stade du 26 Mars in Bamako on Friday, November 13, in the third round of Group K in the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers, with kickoff at 19:00 GMT.

Both sides won their opening two games and sit on six points with a goal difference of +3, Rwanda ahead on goals scored (five to four), and only the top two in a group with no host nation reach the finals in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda.

Anthony Da Silva's first competitive game in charge of Les Aigles ended in a 3-1 home win over Cape Verde, a side who played at this summer's World Cup, on September 25.

Ange Martial Tia scored after five minutes, Sidny Cabral equalised in the 10th minute, and Nene Dorgeles then scored in the 39th and 51st minutes.

Tia also scored the only goal in Paynesville on September 29, in the 79th minute, after which Da Silva said Liberia had defended well on a synthetic pitch.

A 1-1 friendly draw with Morocco in Tangier on October 4, in which Gaoussou Diarra cancelled out Abdessamad Ezzalzouli's 35th-minute penalty in the 77th minute, leaves Mali unbeaten in their last three games.

Mali have never lost to Rwanda, winning three and drawing one of four World Cup qualifiers, with a 7-2 aggregate goal record.

The latest two meetings were a 1-0 home win on September 1, 2021 and a 3-0 win in Kigali on November 11, 2021, yet Da Silva has still described the chances of the two teams as equal.

The Amavubi began with a 3-1 win over Liberia in Kigali on September 25, with Abeddy Biramahire scoring in the second minute, Leroy Mickels in the 33rd and Joy-Lance Mickels from the penalty spot in the 44th.

In Praia on September 29 they trailed to Gilson Benchimol's 40th-minute goal, before Claude Niyomugabo equalised in first-half stoppage time with a long-range strike from a corner.

Elie Tatou Iradukunda scored the winner in the 52nd minute after a mistake by Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha, and Rwanda were outshot 19-6 over the 90 minutes.

Stephen Constantine, in his second spell as Rwanda coach, declared after that win that "the revolution has begun", and his side also drew 0-0 with Kenya on October 5 in an international friendly match in Kigali.

Rwanda are chasing a first AFCON finals appearance since 2004, and Constantine has said he will take one game at a time while rating Group K as containing two of the better teams in Africa.

They have never beaten Mali, scoring only two goals in four meetings, and have conceded in both qualifiers so far.

Mali Africa Cup of Nations Qualifying form:

Rwanda Africa Cup of Nations Qualifying form:

Tia, who has scored twice in two caps for Mali, is out with an ankle injury, while Adama Camara (hamstring) and Lassana Coulibaly (biceps femoris) are also unavailable.

West Ham midfielder Mohamadou Kante receives his first call-up after choosing Mali over France and Senegal, and Swansea City winger Moussa Yeo, 22, is also new after scoring three times in his last five club games.

Gaoussou Diakite of Red Bull Salzburg and Fode Doucoure of Nantes return in a 24-man squad that does not include Yves Bissouma, who joined Ajax in late September, with no reason given for his absence.

For the visitors, Constantine trimmed his squad on Monday, November 9, dropping Elie Ganijuru, Kevin Muhire, Taiba Mbonyumwami and goalkeeper Yves Mugisha, while Fidele Uwiyaremye had already been sent home on the first day of camp for disciplinary reasons.

Defender Thierry Manzi and midfielder Jean Bosco Ruboneka are back after missing the September qualifiers, and Bonheur Mugisha, Gilbert Mugisha and Leroy-Jacques Mickels joined the camp on Monday.

Diarra; Traore, O Camara, Guindo, Gassama; Dieng, Sangare, K. Doumbia; Dorgeles, M. Doumbia, Sinayoko

Mali have not lost to Rwanda in four attempts, and the visitors have not scored against them in either of the last two meetings.

Rwanda's winner in Praia came from a goalkeeping error and they were outshot 19-6 there, while Mali have conceded only Cabral's goal in two games, so chances should be scarce for the Amavubi in Bamako.

Tia's absence removes the scorer of two of Mali's four goals, which is why a narrow margin looks more likely than a repeat of the 3-0 in Kigali in 2021.

Rwanda have scored more than Mali, and with the return leg in Kigali on November 17 a draw in Bamako would suit them.

#1911. Slovakia vs Faroe Islands - prediction, team news, lineups

By Anthony Nolan | 11 Nov 2026 23:07, Last updated: 12 Nov 2026 05:09

Kosicka Futbalova Arena will be the backdrop for a crucial showdown between two unbeaten teams in UEFA Nations League C's Group 3 on Friday, when Slovakia host Faroe Islands.

The Falcons could earn a fourth win in five games, though Landslidid will be motivated by the possibility of promotion.

Vladimir Weiss's Slovakia have produced an impressive campaign in the Nations League, and head into this week's showdown on the cusp of ascension to League B.

The Falcons kicked off their group action with a 2-0 win over Moldova on September 26, which they followed up three days later by beating Kazakhstan 2-1, making it six points from six on home turf.

Weiss's side also hammered Moldova 4-0 in their most recent outing on October 6, though they were held to a 1-1 draw by Friday's opponents prior - the only match the country have failed to triumph in so far.

Ten points from four games have put Slovakia in a commanding position at the top of Nations League Group C3, six clear of second-placed Faroe Islands.

Additionally, the Falcons - who have won four of their last five when playing as the hosts - know that even a draw would be enough to see them secure promotion with room to spare.

Meanwhile, Eydun Klakstein's Faroe Islands may be ranked 126th in the world by FIFA compared to Slovakia's 46th, but they will be cautiously optimistic ahead of this clash.

Landslidid are widely known as international strugglers, but they arrive on the back of a five-game unbeaten run, having yet to taste defeat in this edition of the Nations League.

That remarkable feat has Klakstein's men second in the table, sat in the promotion playoff spot and eyeing an improbable rise through the divisions.

On the other hand, it is notable that Faroe Islands have not come out on top in any of their four Nations League contests so far, even if they remain undefeated, drawing 2-2 with Kazakhstan last time out.

Likewise, Friday's visitors are level on four points with third-placed Moldova, who could usurp them given they are set to face bottom-of-the-pile Kazakhstan.

Slovakia will be lighter in midfield than ideal without Stanislav Lobotka (ankle) and the versatile Tomas Suslov (hamstring), though Peter Pokorny could be joined by Tomas Rigo and Ondrej Duda in the centre of the park.

Further forward, Middlesbrough's David Strelec may lead the attack, supported from out wide by Tomas Bobcek and Lukas Haraslin.

As for Faroe Islands, they are missing Mjallby left wing-back Martin Agnarsson, who is suspended after being sent off against Kazakhstan.

Filling the gaps this week, Klakstein could opt for Samuel Johansen Chukwudi on the left flank, with Joannes Kalso Danielsen on the right.

Elsewhere, Petur Knudsen should be on hand to start up top, supplied by Aki Samuelsen and Hanus Sorensen.

Greif; Mesik, Skriniar, Obert, Hancko; Rigo, Pokorny, Duda; Bobcek, Strelec, Haraslin

Lamhauge; Faero, Vatnhamar, Edmundsson; Danielsen, Turi, Bjartalid, Chukwudi; Samuelsen, Knudsen, Sorensen

Slovakia are the favourites owing to the superior quality in their squad, and their 81-better FIFA ranking, though they are unlikely to pull off a second consecutive thrashing.

Faroe Islands are the only nation that have caused the Falcons to drop points in Group C3, so expect to see another close-fought contest between two unbeaten sides.
